n: In this lesson we will talk about corrosive poisons. Our aim is to learn to distinguish their signs from one another. The plan has five parts. First, the general concept: local action and route of intake. Then acids: mechanism, clinical picture and post-mortem signs. After that, acetic acid and phenol: resorptive action and special features. The fourth part is alkalis, liquefaction necrosis and ammonium. Finally, other substances: formalin, permanganate, peroxide and iodine.

Briefly on the first section. The main action of corrosive poisons is local: a morphological change appears at the site of contact. At the same time, certain general changes are also observed. These substances are most often taken by mouth. In homicide they are rarely encountered. Therefore the distinguishing feature of this group is, first of all, injury at the site of contact.

The second section: acids, in brief. Of the acids, the most common is acetic acid. The damaging factor is free hydrogen ions. They cause coagulation, that is, dry, necrosis. On the body, the main sign is parchment-like streaks around the mouth. Remember: in acid poisoning the necrosis is dry.

Let us look at the frequency of acid poisoning. Acetic acid is relatively common and in most cases is used as a method of suicide. Other acids are rare. They usually lead to accidental poisoning, that is, through an accident. Thus, in practice the main attention is directed to acetic acid.

t: Mechanism of local action of an acid
n: The mechanism of local action of an acid proceeds in sequence. First, free hydrogen ions act on the tissue. As a result the tissue is dehydrated. Then the proteins coagulate. Finally, coagulation, that is, dry, necrosis is formed. That is, free hydrogen ions damage the tissue, which is why the necrosis is dry.

If an acid is in prolonged contact, deep tissues are also damaged. Necrosis develops in the deep tissues. The wall of blood vessels is eroded. The blood clots and undergoes haemolysis. Haemoglobin is converted into acid haematin and methaemoglobin. Another derivative is haematoporphyrin. These processes show that the action of the acid does not remain superficial.

In acid poisoning a dry and dense eschar forms at the site of necrosis. Its colour is brown-black or brown-brownish. Such colour is linked with haemoglobin derivatives. Around the eschar, signs of inflammation are observed. Thus the density and colour of the eschar are an important sign of acid action.

In the clinical picture of acids, local pain and general acidosis go together. There is severe burning pain in the oesophagus and stomach. The vomit contains blood and particles of sloughed mucosa. Oedema and spasm of the glottis develop in the larynx. In general terms, acidosis and metabolic disturbance are observed.

Causes of death from acids are divided into early and late. In the first hours shock, asphyxia and internal haemorrhage lead to death. In late periods pneumonia and acute hepatic and renal failure are responsible. After perforation, mediastinitis or peritonitis may also develop. Remember this distinction.

Inorganic and organic acids differ in dissociation. Inorganic acids dissociate strongly, so free hydrogen ions damage the tissue. Organic acids dissociate weakly, and with them the whole molecule damages. As a result superficial necrosis and marked inflammation appear. That is, the degree of dissociation determines the character of the action.

The lethal dose of acids depends on concentration. For concentrated sulphuric and nitric acids it is 5–10 ml. For hydrochloric acid 15–20 ml. For acetic essence, that is, 40–80%, 20–40 ml. For carbolic acid 10–30 ml. As you see, the lethal amount differs according to the type of acid.

Let us look at the external signs of the body. Around the mouth and on the front of the neck there are yellowish-grey-brown streaks. On palpation their consistency recalls parchment. The mucosa of the lips and mouth is hardened and grey in tone. These signs help to suggest acid poisoning at external examination alone.

In the internal organs of the body the mucosa is hardened, sloughed and ulcerated. The oesophagus is slightly hardened and unevenly thickened. In the stomach the mucosa is sloughed and there are ulcers. In the duodenum and the beginning of the small intestine there is marked oedema and congestion. In the airways the mucosa at the entrance to the larynx is swollen. In the internal organs, congestion and parenchymatous degeneration occur.

The colour of the gastric mucosa differs according to the acid. With sulphuric acid it is brown-black. With nitric acid, if the concentration is above 30%, a yellowish colour appears; this is the xanthoproteic reaction. With a low concentration of nitric acid it is brown-grey. With hydrochloric acid it is also brown-grey. Thus colour helps in identifying the acid.

Each acid has its own predominant sign. With sulphuric acid the stomach wall is damaged and perforation may occur. With hydrochloric and acetic acids volatility is important: oedema of the larynx and lungs appears. Nitric acid, through its nitrogen oxides, gives a suffocating odour. The consequence of nitric acid is toxic pulmonary oedema, bronchitis and pneumonia.

The resorptive action of acetic acid. Its haemolytic action is stronger than that of other acids. First, haemolysis of the blood occurs. Then nephrosis with haemoglobinuria develops. Finally, acute renal failure appears. Remember: with acetic acid the process runs from haemolysis to renal failure.

We now turn to other signs of acetic acid. In the liver necrosis and haemorrhages occur. On aspiration of vapour the airways are damaged and pneumonia develops. The odour of the body is also characteristic: a sharp smell of vinegar comes from the internal organs. This odour is regarded as an important sign for forensic examination.

Causes of death from acetic acid are also divided into two periods. In the early period the cause is exotoxic shock and mechanical asphyxia due to laryngeal oedema. After some time internal haemorrhage, acute renal failure and pneumonia lead to death. Thus first shock and asphyxia, then organ failure.

On phenol and carbolic acid. Phenol is a strong nerve-protoplasmic poison. Carbolic acid is a 90% aqueous solution of phenol. It is relatively rare. The poison can enter through the mouth, respiratory tract and even healthy skin. The form of action is by the whole molecule. This is one of the features distinguishing phenol from acids.

t: Phenol: clinical picture and causes of death
n: The clinical picture of phenol and causes of death. In a short time the central nervous system is damaged and coma develops. Death in the first hours is from paralysis of the respiratory centre. After several days the cause is acute renal failure or respiratory failure. That is, the cause of death changes with time.

The post-mortem signs of phenol depend on the route by which the poison entered. On the gastric mucosa and the skin there is a whitish-grey dry burn. An odour characteristic of carbolic acid comes from the internal organs. Numerous small haemorrhages are found in the brain. In the liver, kidneys and lungs, degeneration, nephrosis and bronchopneumonia occur. The urine on standing in air takes on a green-brown tint; this is hydroquinone-quinhydrone.

The third section: alkalis, in brief. Alkalis cause liquefaction necrosis. They are relatively rare and accidental. The main alkalis are potassium, sodium and ammonium hydroxide. The acting factor is hydroxyl anions. The type of necrosis is liquefactive, that is, wet. This differs from the dry necrosis with acids.

The lethal dose of alkalis differs according to the alkali. For potassium hydroxide it is 10–15 g. For sodium hydroxide also 10–15 g. For ammonium hydroxide, that is, spirit of ammonia, 25–40 ml. Remember: ammonium hydroxide is given not in grams but in millilitres.

t: Mechanism of local action of an alkali
n: The mechanism of local action of an alkali. Hydroxyl anions act on protein and fat. As a result proteins undergo hydrolysis, and fats are saponified. Finally liquefaction necrosis is formed. That is, an alkali does not dry the tissue; on the contrary, it liquefies it.

We compare the differences between acid and alkali. The necrosis is coagulative, that is, dry, with acid, and liquefactive with alkali. The eschar is dry and dense with acid, soft and swollen with alkali. Blood clots with acid and does not clot with alkali. Haemoglobin is converted to acid haematin with acid and to alkaline haematin with alkali. The general shift is acidosis with acid and alkalosis with alkali.

An alkali penetrates deep into the tissue. Tissue protein liquefies and dissolves; this is alkali albuminate. The damaged area is soft, swollen and slippery. The wall of blood vessels undergoes erosion and the blood does not clot. Haemoglobin is converted to alkaline haematin. The necrotic tissue takes on a brown tint.

t: Alkalis: general action and clinical picture
n: The clinical picture of alkalis is similar to that of acids. In general action, alkalosis develops, a metabolic disturbance linked with cations. In the clinical picture there is severe pain in the oesophagus and stomach, and a metallic taste is felt in the mouth. The vomit is brown. In a large dose, shock and collapse occur. After several days pneumonia, mediastinitis and peritonitis develop.

The signs in a body after alkali poisoning. The mucosa is swollen, soft and tears easily. On the skin around the mouth there is a chemical burn in the form of streaks. The oesophagus and pharynx are swollen, grey-green. The stomach is swollen, soft and tears easily. At the beginning of the small intestine the changes are milder. In the larynx and lungs, oedema, congestion and focal pneumonia occur.

Causes of death from alkalis range from burn shock to organ failure. In the early period burn shock, mechanical asphyxia and acute heart failure lead to death. After several days internal haemorrhage, pneumonia, peritonitis, mediastinitis and hepatorenal failure are responsible.

Ammonium hydroxide, that is, spirit of ammonia, deserves special attention. The local action is weak, the resorptive action strong. If drunk together with alcohol, the effects are added. With potassium and sodium hydroxide the local action is stronger. With ammonium hydroxide the local action is weaker; after absorption into the blood it stimulates the CNS. The respiratory centre may be disturbed. Cough, rhinorrhoea and pulmonary oedema are also observed.

The signs in a body after ammonium hydroxide poisoning. The characteristic odour of ammonia comes from the internal organs. There are congestion and haemorrhages on the mucous membranes. In the stomach there is a brown tint in places; its cause is alkaline haematin. When the process is prolonged, necrotic nephrosis develops.

t: Section 4: other corrosive substances, in brief
n: The fourth section: other corrosive substances, in brief. Four substances are considered here. Formaldehyde, that is, formalin, is used in industry, for specimens and for disinfection. Potassium permanganate is widely used in medicine. Hydrogen peroxide is used in canning, the textile industry and medicine. Iodine preparations are met with in medical practice.

Poisoning with formaldehyde and formalin. Formalin is a 37–40% solution of formaldehyde. It is drunk by mistake or with suicidal intent. Local and general action appear together: CNS disturbance and degeneration are observed. In rapid death a characteristic odour is noticed in the internal organs. The mucosa may remain unchanged; when the course is longer, inflammation appears.

Potassium permanganate is a strong oxidising agent. Poisoning occurs accidentally when it is taken by mouth or introduced into the uterus. In the clinical picture there are a burning sensation in the mouth, pain and vomiting. Laryngeal oedema and cardiac weakness are also observed. The lethal dose by mouth is 15–20 g.

The signs in a body after potassium permanganate poisoning. A brownish-reddish burn eschar is characteristic in the oesophagus and stomach. Degenerative changes occur in parenchymatous organs. Toxic bronchopneumonia develops in the lungs. When the course is longer, phlegmon of the stomach may occur.

On hydrogen peroxide. The dangerous solution is 33%, that is, perhydrol. Dangerous amount: 100 ml may lead to death. In the clinical picture, loss of consciousness and bloody foam are observed. Later bloody vomiting and laryngeal oedema appear. In the general condition, respiratory and cardiovascular failure develop.

The signs in a body after hydrogen peroxide poisoning. The mucous membranes of the pharynx, larynx, oesophagus and stomach are swollen and look whitish. The characteristic sign is frothing of the mucosa due to gas bubbles. As a complication, the stomach wall may rupture from the gas.

Iodine preparations: tincture of iodine and Lugol's solution. With local action a brown eschar forms on the mucosa. In the heart and lungs, disturbance up to collapse and toxic oedema are observed. Proteinuria and haematuria are found in the urine. In the liver and kidneys there are severe degenerative changes. When taken by mouth, an asphyxial state appears due to laryngeal oedema.

t: Teaching case 1: streaks around the mouth
n: The first teaching case: streaks around the mouth. This is a hypothetical case, not a real examination. The given signs: parchment-like streaks around the mouth, a sharp smell of vinegar from the internal organs, haemolysis of the blood and kidney damage. Questions: which substance is likely, which action is strong, and what is the initial cause of death? Try to answer yourself.

The answer to the first case: the set of signs corresponds to acetic acid. The likely substance is acetic acid. The strong action is resorptive, haemolytic. The kidney damage is nephrosis with haemoglobinuria. The initial cause of death is exotoxic shock and asphyxia. Confirmation, however, is obtained by laboratory examination.

The second teaching case: soft, swollen stomach. This is a hypothetical case, not a real examination. Given: the stomach is soft and tears easily, the mucosa is grey-green and swollen, and uncoagulated blood flows from the vessel. Questions: acid or alkali, what is the type of necrosis, which sign is decisive? First think for yourself.

t: Case 2 answer: consistent with an alkali
n: The answer to the second case: the signs correspond to the action of an alkali. The likely group is alkalis. The necrosis is liquefactive. The reason is the soft wall and the non-clotting blood. Haemoglobin has been converted to alkaline haematin. The general shift is alkalosis.

Conclusion: the main sign and danger for each group. Acids have dry necrosis and a brown-black eschar. Acetic acid is characterised by haemolysis, nephrosis and a sharp smell of vinegar. Phenol has CNS damage, dry burn and hydroquinone-quinhydrone. Alkalis have soft, swollen tissue and non-clotting blood. Of the others, formalin fixes, while peroxide produces foam.

The review questions rest on the slides of the lesson. On acids: what are the mechanism of necrosis and the properties of the eschar? On acetic acid: why is the haemolytic action important? On phenol: what are the causes of death and the colour of the urine? On alkalis: how do they differ from acids? On other substances: what are the signs of formalin and peroxide?
